title: Forgiving institutions
hookLine: forgiving a church, a company, a country is different from forgiving a person

cards: A hospital billing office. A school that looked away. A congregation that closed ranks.
A company that laid off a whole floor by email. A government office that lost the file, again. When the hurt comes from one of these, who exactly is there to forgive?
The receptionist didn't write the policy. The pastor who's there now wasn't there then. The building can't apologize.

teach.b: First, a prayer in the plural. In the book of Daniel, Daniel prays for his whole people: "We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled." We, not I.
He names the kings, the princes and the fathers who came before him, and still says we. In Daniel's prayer, wrong can belong to a group, not just to one person. Second, the trouble.
When a person hurts you, you can forgive that person. When an institution hurts you, the hurt is spread across a policy, a culture, many hands and a lot of silence.
Forgiving it can feel like trying to hug fog. Third, a way through.
Henry David Thoreau, in his essay on civil disobedience, observes that it's said a corporation has no conscience, but a corporation of conscientious people has one. Institutions are made of people.

Some find it possible to release bitterness toward the individuals inside, who may be doing their best, while still naming what the institution as a whole did. Fourth, forgiveness isn't dropping the matter.
You can let go of the poison you carry about a church, a company or a country, and still write the letter, file the complaint, vote, or speak up so it doesn't happen to the next person.

In Daniel, the confession and the plea for things to be put right come in the same breath. In this way of seeing it, the letting go is for the one who was hurt, and the accountability is for whoever comes next.

how: Jews and Christians read Daniel 9 as a model of confessing wrongs on behalf of a whole people, and some communities and institutions today issue collective apologies for past harms while victims decide for themselves whether and how to forgive.

o: forgiving the whole group because one person there apologized
deciding no one is to blame because many people were involved
letting go of bitterness at a group, while still asking it to own up

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.

s: Daniel's prayer confesses only his own personal wrongs
he prays in the plural: "We have sinned."
Thoreau observes that a corporation of conscientious people has a conscience
forgiving an institution means you can't complain or seek change
you can let go of the bitterness and still speak up.

games.q: you're Daniel, praying about wrongs done by your people, their kings and their fathers before you. how do you pray?
o: say it was their fault, not yours.
confess it in the plural: we have sinned.
say nothing about the past at all.
games.why: Daniel says "we": "We have sinned, and have committed iniquity." he speaks for the whole people.

practice: Name silently one institution that has hurt you, a school, a workplace, a religious community, an agency, and notice where the anger sits in your body.
Picture one ordinary person inside it who had nothing to do with what happened to you, and see if you can let just them off the hook.
Then, separately, name one thing you'd still want the institution to own or change; both can stay true.

wordCard.voice: Forgiving institutions. Releasing bitterness toward a group with no single face, while still asking it to own what it did. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: bigger than one. Kindness for the person in front of you, the complaint for the place it belongs. See you tomorrow.
